data.title: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 against the Slavs
data.excerpt: In the Early Middle Ages the Slavic tribes of the Elbe region and the Baltic coast held powerful principalities in what is now Germany, and many of them still kept their pagan faith in the 12th century. In 1147 Christendom sent two armies against them – the Wendish Crusade. This article, translated from a Russian original, follows the campaign from Niklot's raid on Lübeck through the sieges of Dobín and Dymín to the ignominious collapse of the whole enterprise.
data.metaTitle: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 against the Slavs
data.metaDescription: In 1147 two crusading armies marched against the pagan Elbe and Pomeranian Slavs. Niklot's defence of Dobín turned the campaign into a fiasco.

timeline.title: The first plan for the campaign
timeline.description: A crusade against the Western Slavs was already intended shortly after the First Crusade to Constantinople, but at that time it did not take place.

timeline.title: The missions of Otto of Bamberg
timeline.description: The Christian bishop Otto of Bamberg twice visited the land of the Pomeranian Slavs with the aim of converting them to Christianity.

timeline.title: The Wendish Crusade
timeline.description: Christendom sent two armies against the Elbe and Pomeranian Slavs – one against the Obodrites, the other against the Liutizi.

timeline.title: Niklot's attack on Lübeck
timeline.description: Niklot, prince of the Obodrites, took Lübeck in a sudden attack from the sea and destroyed the ships anchored in the harbour, thwarting the crusaders' operational base.

timeline.title: The siege of Dobín
timeline.description: German and Danish forces besieged Niklot's fortification of Dobín; meanwhile the Rani defeated the Danish fleet at sea and the supplying of the besiegers was stopped.

timeline.title: The retreat from Dymín
timeline.description: After the failure before Dymín and the loss of his hopes of gaining Rujana, the Abbot of Corvey returned home from the campaign.

timeline.title: The fall of Brandenburg
timeline.description: The principality of Brandenburg was taken by means of intrigue and deceit, and the German advance eastwards continued.

timeline.title: The end of the Obodrite state
timeline.description: During a further invasion the Obodrite state restored by Niklot came to an end, and Niklot himself perished in a trap.

children.text: As we know, in the Early Middle Ages extensive territories in the area of present-day Germany (the Elbe region and the Baltic coast) were inhabited by Slavic tribes which had built powerful principalities there. Moreover, a number of these tribes still kept their original pagan faith in the 12th century. This fact (together with the desire to gain power over their extensive territories) stuck in the throats of many Christian rulers and commanders and eventually led to the so-called Wendish Crusade. You can read about this event in the following article, which is a translation from a Russian original:

The following text is a literal translation of an older article from a Russian source (the leva-net.webnode.cz portal, the original Russian text at peshera.org). The historical core of the translation draws on authentic medieval chronicles – above all Helmold's Chronicle of the Slavs and the testimony of Bishop Otto of Bamberg – and on the study by the historian N. Gracianskij “The crusade of 1147 against the Slavs and its results”. In some places, however, the translation also takes over references to the pseudo-historical literature of N. Levashov and the concept of the so-called “Slavic-Aryan empire”, which have no support in scholarly historiography. We reproduce them only as an inseparable part of the original translation, without identifying ourselves with them.

blocks.text: The Wagrians, like the other West Slavic tribes, met an unenviable fate. At the beginning of the 10th century the German Drang nach Osten (drive to the east) began, in the course of which the Western Slavs were partly driven out of their lands, partly converted to Christianity and assimilated, but most of them were simply exterminated.
blocks.author: prof. N. Gracianskij (after Helmold and Otto of Bamberg)

blocks.text:
In 1147 Christendom organised the Second Crusade, also called the Wendish Crusade, and sent crusaders against the Elbe Slavs, despite the fact that many of the Elbe and Pomeranian Slavic lands were by that time already Christian, at least formally.

As can be seen, religious motives were not the only reason for the campaign. The parasitic dark forces that stood behind the process of the spiritual and physical extermination of the Slavs used every means (on the reasons for the extermination of the Slavs in particular see N. Levashov's book “The Mirror of My Soul”, vol. 3, ch. 1). They thus also made use of the German, Danish and Polish dukes, margraves and other representatives of the “European elite”, who had become part of it comparatively recently, after the West European territories had gradually been separated from the Slavic-Aryan empire, and of their desire to sink their claws into Slavic wealth. They were given no peace by the Slavic “land broad, rich in grain and in fat pastures, abounding in fish, meat and all manner of goods…”, as the 12th-century Christian missionary Helmold (Gemold) noted in his “Chronicle of the Slavs”.

All the Christian chroniclers report that the Slavs lived well and prosperously. And although they regarded the pagan Slavs with the conceit of fanatics, certain of the exclusiveness and the superiority of their own faith, even they note the outstanding human qualities of the Slavs. The same Helmold writes:

“… The Prussians have not yet come to know the light of faith; a people possessing many singular good qualities, “most loving of men” towards those suffering want; “they hasten to meet those who are exposed to danger at sea or to persecution by pirates, and come to their aid. For gold and silver they care almost nothing at all. They have an abundance of unknown furs, for which the deadly poison of pride has flooded our land. And they value them as dung, I believe to our reproach, who sigh after a garment of fur as after the greatest happiness. Therefore for linen clothing, which among us is called faldones, they give us such costly furs…”

And here are the words of the Christian bishop Otto of Bamberg, who twice, in 1124 and 1127, visited the land of the Pomeranian Slavs with the aim of converting them to Christianity: “… there is an incredible abundance of fish there, both in the seas and in the rivers, lakes and ponds. For a denarius you could buy a cartload of fresh herring, and were I to begin to tell what I know of their smell and their fatness, I should be accused of gluttony. Throughout the land there are many red deer, fallow deer and wild horses, bears, boars and swine and game of every kind; butter from cows and sheep's milk, fat lambs and rams, with an abundance of honey and wheat, with hemp and poppy, and all kinds of vegetables, and if there were vines, olives and fig trees there, you would think it the promised land, so many fruit trees are there in it…
blocks.author: prof. N. Gracianskij (after Helmold and Otto of Bamberg)

blocks.text:
Honesty and friendship among them are such that they know neither theft nor deceit at all; their chests and caskets they leave unlocked. In fact we saw no locks or keys there, and they themselves were greatly astonished when they saw our bags and caskets locked. Their clothes, their money and all their valuables they put away in their barrels and vessels, simply covered with a lid, and they fear no deceit, because they have not experienced it…”

And so in 1147 there began the crusade against the Western Slavs that had already been intended in 1107–1108, shortly after the First Crusade to Constantinople (see N. Levashov, “The Mirror of My Soul”, vol. 2, chapter 5). A description of this campaign is given in the extensive article by Professor N. Gracianskij “The crusade of 1147 against the Slavs and its results”

“… The crusaders decided to march against the Elbe Slavs with two armies: one was to go from the lower Elbe against the Obodrites, the other from Magdeburg against the Liutizi. At the head of the first army stood Henry the Lion, Conrad, Duke of Burgundy, Adalbert, Archbishop of Bremen, Dittmar, Bishop of Bremen, and others. This army was to be joined by the Danes, led by both their kings – Sweyn and Knut – who had decided to end their internal quarrels for the sake of action against their common enemies, the Obodrites.

At the head of the second army stood, among the secular princes, the Count Palatine Frederick of Saxony, Herman of the Rhine, the margraves Albert the Bear and Conrad of Meissen, and among the ecclesiastical princes, besides the papal legate, the Bishop of Havelberg, also Frederick, Archbishop of Magdeburg, the bishops of Halberstadt, Merseburg, Brandenburg and Münster, and also Wibald, Abbot of Corvey. The latter had designs on the island of Rujana, basing his claims on an old absurd version according to which the Svantovít worshipped on the island was St Vitus deified by the Slavs, the patron of the monastery of Corvey, to which one of the German kings had supposedly granted the island. Only the unshakeable confidence of the Germans in success could have brought the abbot to set out beyond the Elbe and thus prevent the rights of his monastery from being infringed in the anticipated division of Slavic territory.

On the number of crusaders who marched against the Slavs we have the following figures: the northern army is said to have numbered 40,000 men, the southern 60,000 and the Danish 100,000. These figures are indeed greatly exaggerated, but in any case they show that an enormous, hitherto unseen German-Danish host set out beyond the Elbe, which was to put an end once and for all to the independence of the Slavs and to their paganism. In the face of so terrible a threat, however, the Slavs did not lose heart and had no intention whatever of submitting to the Germans. The chief hero of the defence against the enemy was the courageous Niklot, prince of the Obodrites. Helmold decidedly has no love for Niklot and is not always just in his judgements of him, but what he says of the deeds of this prince clearly shows his gift as a commander. “When he heard that an army would soon gather for his destruction,” we read in Helmold, “Niklot called together all his people and began to build the fortification of Dobín, so that it might be a shelter for the people in case of need…”

At the same time Niklot sought allies for the coming struggle and turned to Count Adolf of Holstein, reminding him of the agreement they had concluded. Although Adolf had no sympathy for the crusade, he naturally refused to help Niklot against his own duke, Henry the Lion, and the prince's only allies became the Rani.

Relying on his alliance with the warlike seafarers, Niklot worked out, as the following events show, an excellent plan of defence. By a whole series of combined actions on land and at sea he intended to defeat the crusaders by starvation and thereby thwart all their predatory plans. Niklot's first objective was the destruction of the crusaders' presumed nearest operational base in Wagria. In a sudden attack from the sea Niklot took Lübeck on 29 June and destroyed the ships anchored in the harbour, whereby “the men, drunk from heavy drinking, could not rise from their beds and ships until the enemy had surrounded them and, setting fire, had destroyed the ships laden with goods. And on that day some 300 men and more were killed.”
blocks.author: prof. N. Gracianskij (after Helmold and Otto of Bamberg)

blocks.text:
Having thus destroyed the ships in the harbour of Lübeck and given the town over to the flames, Niklot sent out two detachments of horsemen who rode through the whole land of the Wagrians and killed or captured the German colonists settled there. Only the colonists from Holstein, who dwelt west of the upper course of the Trave, were for some reason left untouched by the Slavs. Perhaps Niklot wished to sow discord among the Germans and to cast suspicion on the Holsteiners that they had acted in concert with the Slavs. If so, then Niklot achieved his aim brilliantly, for suspicion of treason did indeed fall on the Holsteiners…

The first result of the crusade against the Slavs, proclaimed at the Diet of Frankfurt, was thus the destruction of a prosperous German trading town on the Baltic and the almost complete annihilation of the colonists who had been gathered with great difficulty from various parts of Germany and the Netherlands to settle conquered Wagria. In their bold raid the Slavs apparently suffered no losses; they returned to their ships and “sailed away, laden with captives and with various goods which they had taken as spoil in the land of the Wagrians.”

Niklot's unexpected diversionary action naturally caused great commotion among the Germans, and the crusading army hastened to invade the land of the Slavs “in order to curb their violence.” Niklot emptied and laid waste the territory of his principality through which the crusaders had to pass, and settled himself with a quantity of provisions and large forces in Dobín. The German forces which had set out against the Obodrites from the lower Elbe were probably already before Dobín in July. The Danes also hurried there; their fleet landed on the Slavic coast apparently in the Bay of Wismar, not far from Lake Schwerin, on which Dobín lay.

The first to sail in were the Goths with their king Knut and the Jutes (Schleswigers) with king Sweyn. Then came Sweyn's subjects, the Zealanders and the Scanians. After landing, the greater part of the Danish forces joined the Saxons before Dobín, while the other part remained to guard the ships. Niklot, fortified in Dobín, was able to carry out the second part of his well-considered plan of defence, namely to cut the crusaders' sea routes and to strike at the Danish fleet, which was probably supplying the besiegers, since the land of the Obodrites, abandoned by its inhabitants, and devastated Wagria were unable to feed the crusading host. Besides, land communication was generally difficult to use because of the marshy character of the terrain.

Niklot solved this task brilliantly with the help of the Rani seafarers. In Helmold we read: “When the besieged once saw that the army of the Danes was acting hesitantly – for they are brave soldiers only at home, and in a foreign land they are not distinguished by bravery – they made an unexpected sortie, killed many of them and manured the earth with their bodies. It was not possible to help them, since a lake lay between (the armies)…”

Niklot's actions on land and those of the Rani at sea proceeded simultaneously and in coordination: Niklot had to divert the attention of the Danish army from the ships and thus help the Rani to victory. This aim was achieved, and the Rani had no less success at sea than the Obodrites on land… The whole Scanian fleet fell to the victors, and the Rani thus doubled their forces…

Although a considerable part of the Danish fleet survived, the sea was now controlled by the Rani. The supplying of the army lying before Dobín therefore had to be stopped, and the host was threatened with famine. This cooled the crusaders' enthusiasm for battle and they began to think of retreat. The Danes, burning with the desire to avenge themselves on Niklot for their defeat, no sooner learned of the Rani attack than they changed their intention and hurried to their ships. It seems that they did not return to Dobín at all and sailed home without delay; and as for the remaining Saxons before the fortress, they began to speak of the pointlessness of the campaign, of the senselessness of laying waste a land that paid tribute to the Germans. “Is not the land we are laying waste,” the Saxons are said to have asked, “our own land? And are not the people we are fighting our own people? Why then should we be enemies to ourselves and squander the tribute they pay us? Does this not bring losses to our rulers as well… ”

As can be seen, the Germans grasped the senselessness of their undertaking only after the Slavs had given them a hard lesson, which showed that instead of the expected easy spoil, nothing but hardship awaited the greedy crusaders in the Slavic land…

The main (southern) crusading army assembled, as agreed, at Magdeburg… The main direction of the whole campaign was evidently set by Albert the Bear, who wished with the help of the crusaders to extend the boundaries of his Northern March beyond the Peene and the Oder. Otto of Bamberg had already spread Christianity there, but it must be borne in mind that the princes concealed this fact from the masses of crusaders, arousing their greed with the prospect of rich spoil among the pagans, against whom everything was permitted. The ecclesiastical princes competed with the secular ones in their plans of war, while the head of the prelates, the Archbishop of Magdeburg, longed to subordinate the independent Pomeranian bishopric and to gain control of its enormous revenues from wealthy Pomerania…

The army marched into Pomerania by the same road that Otto of Bamberg had taken 20 years before. With great difficulty the crusaders passed through the dense forest that separates the territory of the Stodorani (Hevelli) from the Morichani, and reached Lake Müritz in pagan territory which recognised neither the Germans nor Christianity. The inhabitants fled, saving what they could, and the crusaders plundered and burned the Slavic settlements. In the course of this the Slavic town of Malchin was also burned down, together with the pagan sanctuary before its gates. Marking its way with looting, arson and murder, the army set out for Dymín – a town of the Liutizi on the Peene – but before it reached the town it divided: part of the host headed for Szczecin.

Before Dymín the crusaders unexpectedly met with the same resistance from the Slavs as before Dobín. We do not know exactly what happened here, but from certain indications we may judge that on the Peene the crusaders suffered the same failure as among the Obodrites before Dobín. It is no accident that Helmold joins the events before both Slavic fortresses into a single account of the failure of the crusade. There are also further reports of discord and of the failure of the crusaders before Dymín. The clearest indicator of this failure is the behaviour of the Abbot of Corvey, who quickly took leave of his dreams of gaining Rujana and as early as 8 September returned home from the campaign. Expressing his joy at having escaped the danger in the Slavic land, the abbot says that the campaign, though fruitless, was at any rate carried out “with obedience”…

Complete failure also befell the army that set out against Szczecin, the capital of Pomerania. When the crusaders besieged the town, the besieged displayed crosses on the town ramparts as a sign that they were Christians, and confusion then reigned among the host. It began to be clear to all that the enterprise they had organised stood in glaring contradiction to the ideas preached by Bernard of Clairvaux and by the pope, and the rank-and-file crusaders understood that they had been deceived by the princes, who wished by their hands to seize new lands and new revenues not from pagans but from Christians…

This broadly conceived crusade against the Slavs thus came to ignominious grief in everything, and contemporaries had no doubt whatever about it: almost all of them unanimously comment on the complete failure of the Germans' campaign beyond the Elbe. Some explain the failure of the campaign by the quarrel among the princes, others by ignorance of the enemy terrain, still others by the fact that the crusaders were not defending “God's cause” but were guided by purely predatory intentions. In reality the campaign failed thanks to the heroic resistance of the Slavs, and the princes' quarrels themselves and the disintegration of the army began only after the Germans had unexpectedly come up against strong Slavic fortresses whose defenders resolutely faced the German plunderers. In the end, even before Szczecin the matter was decided not by the crosses placed on the town ramparts, but by the formidable appearance of the fortification of Szczecin, defended by a valiant Slavic garrison…”

Unfortunately, the German advance eastwards did not stop there. In 1150 the principality of Brandenburg was taken by means of intrigue and deceit. Wagria was gradually and persistently Christianised through the creeping infiltration of immigrants from Germany and the Netherlands. The only one who still resisted Christian aggression was the Obodrite prince Niklot. After the Christian campaign he succeeded in restoring the old state of the Obodrites within its original borders, with the exception of Wagria and the Elbe region occupied by the Germans, and in subjugating the neighbouring coastal tribes of the Liutizi – the Kessini and the Circipani. Unfortunately, the union of the Liutizi and the Obodrites proved fragile, and Niklot, after failing to come to terms with the kindred Slavic tribes, made a fatal mistake: in order to subjugate the Liutizi, he turned to the Germans. Fire and sword swept through the land of the Liutizi, which meant that there could no longer be any question of uniting the northern Elbe tribes into an independent Slavic state.

Nor was the Obodrite state restored by Niklot stable; it held together only thanks to external pressure. It came to an end in 1160 during a further invasion. Niklot himself also perished then, when he fell into a trap. Niklot's last battle is described in the “History of Mecklenburg” as follows: “Niklot, with a few daring men of his retinue, made a sortie from the fortress. They lay in ambush not far from the enemy camp. Soon a supply detachment appeared from the camp of the Saxons to procure provisions – food. Among the servants were mingled knights who concealed their armour beneath simple outer clothing… Niklot threw himself impetuously into the throng of the enemy, suspecting no trick, and thrust his spear into one of them, but the point glanced off the invisible armour. Then Niklot understood that he had been deceived. He tried to escape to his own men, but it was already too late. The enemy horsemen overtook him, and before help could reach him he was killed… ”

Thus the political fragmentation of the Western Slavs led to their almost complete extermination…
